raw.title: `toJSONSchema()`: chaining `.int()` after `.min()`/`.max()` replaces explicit bounds
v4.5 : safeParse() can crash with a `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`
Regression in 4.5.0: nested recursive `discriminatedUnion` throws `Maximum call stack size exceeded`
raw.body:
### Summary

A `discriminatedUnion` that reaches itself through a getter throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` in 4.5.x — but only when the union is **nested inside another schema**. As the root schema it parses fine, and in 4.4.3 it parses fine either way.

This is the same shape as #4444 (closed) and produces the same `escapeRegex` → `$ZodLiteral.init` frame as #4994 (closed), so it looks like a regression of a bug that was fixed once.

### Reproduction

zod only, no other dependencies:

```js
import * as z from "zod";

const Geometry = () =>
  z.discriminatedUnion("type", [
    z.object({ type: z.literal("Point"), coordinates: z.array(z.number()) }),
    z.looseObject({
      type: z.literal("GeometryCollection"),
      get geometries() {
        return z.array(Geometry());
      },
    }),
  ]);

const point = { type: "Point", coordinates: [1, 2] };

Geometry().safeParse(point); // ok

z.object({ geometry: Geometry() }).safeParse({ geometry: point }); // RangeError
```

| zod | as the root | nested in an object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4.4.3 | ok (1 ms) | ok (1 ms) |
| 4.5.0 | ok (2 ms) | **RangeError** |
| 4.5.4 | ok (1 ms) | **RangeError** |

Any nesting triggers it — `z.object`, `z.looseObject`, `z.array`, `.optional()`, `.nullable()`. A plain `z.union([z.string(), Geometry()])` does not.

### Stack

```
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at String.replace (<anonymous>)
    at Module.escapeRegex (zod/v4/core/util.js:260:16)
    at zod/v4/core/schemas.js:1890:55
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at zod/v4/core/schemas.js:1890:14
    at $ZodLiteral.init (zod/v4/core/core.js:65:9)
```

### Impact

[`zod-geojson`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/zod-geojson) composes `GeoJSONFeatureSchema` and `GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema` exactly this way, so on 4.5.x both spend about eight seconds and then throw — on an empty feature collection, before any real data is involved:

```js
import { GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema } from "zod-geojson";

GeoJSONFeatureCollectionSchema.safeParse({ type: "FeatureCollection", features: [] });
// ~8 s, then RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Its simple schemas (`GeoJSONPointSchema`, `GeoJSONLineStringSchema`, `GeoJSONGeometrySchema`) are unaffected and parse in ~2 ms. Both zod-geojson 1.7.0 and 1.7.1 behave identically, so the version of that package is not the variable.

For a browser app this is worse than a thrown error: the eight seconds are spent on the main thread, so the UI freezes before the parse fails.

### Environment

- zod 4.5.0, 4.5.1, 4.5.2, 4.5.4 — all bad; 4.4.3 good (first bad release: 4.5.0)
- Node v24.14.0, Linux

raw.title: Make util.cached a plain box instead of an accessor literal
toJSONSchema emits a base64url pattern that accepts strings z.base64url() rejects
raw.body:
### Problem

`z.base64url()` and the JSON Schema it generates disagree about the same string:

```ts
z.base64url().safeParse("A").success;              // false
z.toJSONSchema(z.base64url()).pattern;             // "^[A-Za-z0-9_-]*$"  — matches "A"
```

Unpadded base64url encodes 3 bytes per 4 characters, so a length that leaves a remainder of 1 mod 4 carries no whole byte and no encoder can produce it. `regexes.base64` already rules this out; `regexes.base64url` does not.

`isValidBase64URL()` catches it at parse time, so `parse()` is correct. But `$ZodBase64URL` assigns the loose regex to `def.pattern`, and that is what `toJSONSchema()` emits — so a consumer validating against the generated schema accepts input Zod itself rejects. That matters where the schema is handed to something else (tool calling, a gateway) and Zod re-validates afterwards.

### Suggested fix

Give `base64url` the same split `base64` already has — a strict pattern for the schema, a dedicated validator for parsing:

- `regexes.base64url` → `/^(?:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{4})*(?:[A-Za-z0-9_-]{2,3})?$/`, mirroring `regexes.base64`. This is what lands in `def.pattern`.
- a new `regexes.base64urlCharset` (`/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]*$/`) for `isValidBase64URL()`.

The second part is load-bearing: `isValidBase64()` never runs its pattern (it checks `length % 4` and calls `atob`), but `isValidBase64URL()` does run its own against user input of any size, and a quantified group overflows the stack on a long subject — the existing `big base64 and base64url` test (10 MB) hits exactly that. The length rule is already enforced downstream, where the padded string reaches `isValidBase64()`.

### Status

I have this implemented on a branch, with `"A"` added to the existing invalid fixtures in `string.test.ts`. `check:semver`, `check:comments`, `biome check` and the full `packages/zod` suite (7835 tests) pass, and runtime parse behaviour is unchanged.

The change is here, ready to open as a PR: https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/compare/main...oleg6k:zod:fix/base64url-pattern

PR creation is currently limited to collaborators, so I am filing this instead — happy to open the PR as soon as that lifts, or to hand over the diff if someone wants to land it directly.

raw.title: z.emoji() accepts strings that contain no emoji
raw.body:
### Problem

`z.emoji()` accepts strings that contain no emoji at all:

```ts
z.emoji().parse("123");        // passes
z.emoji().parse("#");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("*");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{200D}");   // lone ZWJ, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{FE0F}");   // lone variation selector, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{1F3FD}");  // lone skin tone modifier, passes
```

The pattern is `^[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Emoji_Component}]+$`. `\p{Emoji_Component}` is not a set of emoji — it is the set of pieces that combine with one: ASCII digits `0`–`9`, `#`, `*`, regional indicators, skin tone modifiers, ZWJ and variation selectors. A string built only from components is not an emoji.

### Suggested fix

Keep the character class exactly as it is — the single class matters, #6347 replaced an alternation with it to kill the exponential backtracking over the U+1F9B0–U+1F9B3 overlap — and add a leading lookahead requiring one anchor: an `Extended_Pictographic`, a regional indicator, or U+20E3, the enclosing keycap that makes `1️⃣` an emoji.

```
^(?=[\s\S]*[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Regional_Indicator}⃣])[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Emoji_Component}]+$
```

`[\s\S]` rather than `[^]`, and `⃣` rather than `\u{20E3}`, because the pattern is emitted into JSON Schema and not every consumer parses the ECMAScript-only spellings.

### Checks

- every emoji in `unicode-emoji-json` (1914 entries) still validates, and every existing fixture in `string.test.ts` passes, keycap sequences included
- `recheck` reports the new pattern safe; the lookahead is a single unnested quantifier, so matching stays linear — measured at 1k/10k/50k characters, on both the matching and the failing path, it costs about 10% more than the current pattern and scales linearly
- two snapshots that carry the pattern as text need updating
- full `packages/zod` suite passes (7835 tests)

### Status

Implemented on a branch with tests for the component-only cases above. The change is here, ready to open as a PR: https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/compare/main...oleg6k:zod:fix/emoji-component-only

PR creation is currently limited to collaborators, so I am filing this instead — happy to open the PR as soon as that lifts.

fromJSONSchema silently ignores uniqueItems, contains, minContains and maxContains
raw.body:
All four are listed in `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` (`from-json-schema.ts:70-73`), so they are consumed
rather than falling through to `extraMeta`, but no validation is attached to the converted
schema. The result accepts data the JSON Schema rejects.

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", items: { type: "number" }, uniqueItems: true })
  .safeParse([1, 1]).success                    // true

fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", contains: { type: "number" } })
  .safeParse(["a", "b"]).success                // true

fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", contains: { type: "number" }, minContains: 2 })
  .safeParse([1, "a"]).success                  // true

fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", contains: { type: "number" }, maxContains: 1 })
  .safeParse([1, 2]).success                    // true
```

All four should fail. Checked on `main` at `e6b6ab34` (4.5.2). The array branch records it at
`from-json-schema.ts:534`:

```ts
// TODO: uniqueItems and contains/minContains/maxContains are not supported
```

This is the same shape as #6463 (`minProperties`/`maxProperties`), which #6493 is closing.

### The question, before I write anything

#6493 says explicitly: *"Rather than a converter-only guard, this adds the property count as a
first-class check, so hand-written schemas get it too and `toJSONSchema` can emit it"*, with the
bounds on their own bag keys and every locale gaining an entry.

The same reasoning applies here — there is no `z.uniqueItems()` or `z.contains()` today and
`toJSONSchema` never emits either keyword — so I would rather follow that shape than add a
converter-only guard. Before I do: **is that the direction you want for the array keywords, and
would you want them as one PR or separately from `contains`/`minContains`/`maxContains`?**

### One place the array case genuinely differs

#6493 notes that the property checks count the **parsed** value, *"like every other check"*, so a
key synthesized by a property `default` counts toward the minimum. For arrays that would be wrong,
because JSON Schema `default` is an annotation and does not add an item to the instance:

```ts
// item default 5, so [undefined, 5] parses to [5, 5]
fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", items: { type: "number", default: 5 }, uniqueItems: true })
  .safeParse([undefined, 5])   // must PASS - only one 5 was sent

// [undefined] parses to [5]
fromJSONSchema({ type: "array", items: { type: "number", default: 5 }, contains: { const: 5 } })
  .safeParse([undefined])      // must FAIL - no 5 was sent
```

Counting the parsed array flips both. So whichever shape you prefer, I think the array counts have
to read the input rather than the output. Happy to be told otherwise if you would rather they stay
consistent with the other checks.

I have a working converter-side implementation with tests, but I would rather rewrite it to match
#6493 than send something in the shape you have just moved away from.

raw.title: fromJSONSchema silently ignores minProperties and maxProperties
raw.body:
## `fromJSONSchema` silently ignores `minProperties` and `maxProperties`

Both keywords are listed in `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` in `from-json-schema.ts` (so they are silently consumed instead of falling into `extraMeta`), but no validation logic is ever attached to the resulting schema. An object with `minProperties: 1` accepts `{}`, and one with `maxProperties: 2` accepts three or more keys without error.

### Reproduce

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  type: "object",
  properties: { a: { type: "string" }, b: { type: "number" } },
  minProperties: 1,
  maxProperties: 2,
});

schema.safeParse({}).success      // true  — should be false (0 < minProperties)
schema.safeParse({ a: "x", b: 1, c: true }).success  // true  — should be false (3 > maxProperties)
```

### Expected

Both should fail: `{}` has 0 properties (< `minProperties: 1`), and `{ a, b, c }` has 3 properties (> `maxProperties: 2`).

### Actual

Both parse successfully — the keywords are consumed without effect.

### Root cause

`minProperties` and `maxProperties` appear in the `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` set (lines 62–63 of `from-json-schema.ts`) but are never referenced in `convertBaseSchema` or `convertSchema`. By contrast, the analogous array keywords `minItems`/`maxItems` are applied via `.check(z.minLength(...))` / `.check(z.maxLength(...))`, and string `minLength`/`maxLength` via `.min()` / `.max()`. The object property-count keywords simply have no corresponding branch.

### Fix

Layer a `.check()` on the object schema after `propertyNames` handling, counting `Object.keys(value).length` against the threshold and emitting `too_small` / `too_big` issues with `origin: "object"`. I have a patch ready (37 lines in `from-json-schema.ts` + 40 lines of regression tests in `from-json-schema.test.ts`) — happy to open a PR if `pull_request_creation_policy` allows, or I can attach the diff here.

raw.title: z.toJSONSchema on a fixed-length tuple emits no length constraint
raw.body:
Preview

Code

Blame
64 lines (46 loc) · 3.31 KB
z.toJSONSchema on a fixed-length tuple emits no length constraint
Zod version: 4.4.3

What was expected
z.toJSONSchema(z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()])) should emit a JSON Schema that accepts the same arrays z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()]) accepts — that is, arrays of exactly two elements, a string followed by a number.

What happens
The emitted schema constrains the element types but not the array length, so it accepts arrays that are shorter or longer than the tuple. Validating with Ajv against the declared 2020-12 dialect, three of five probe values are accepted by the JSON Schema and rejected by Zod.

This matters most in tool calling. The emitted JSON Schema is what a language model is shown and what the provider validates the model's arguments against; the original Zod schema is what the application re-checks those arguments with. A JSON Schema that is more permissive than the validator it was generated from produces arguments that pass every check upstream and fail at the application boundary, with nothing in between reporting a problem.

The exact emitted document
{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","type":"array","prefixItems":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"}]}
prefixItems alone places no bound on length in 2020-12. Closing the short side needs minItems: 2; closing the long side needs items: false.

Probe table
probe	zod accepts	JSON Schema accepts	verdict
[]	false	true	wider
["a"]	false	true	wider
["a",1]	true	true	agree
["a",1,2]	false	true	wider
["a","b"]	false	false	agree
Reproduction
mkdir -p /tmp/schema-parity-repro && cd /tmp/schema-parity-repro
npm init -y && npm i -s zod@4.4.3 ajv@8.20.0
node -e '
const {z}=require("zod"), Ajv=require("ajv/dist/2020");
const t=z.tuple([z.string(), z.number()]);
const js=z.toJSONSchema(t);
const ok=new Ajv({strict:false}).compile(js);
console.log(JSON.stringify(js));
for (const v of [[], ["a"], ["a",1], ["a",1,2], ["a","b"]])
  console.log(JSON.stringify(v).padEnd(12), "zod:", String(t.safeParse(v).success).padEnd(5), "json-schema:", ok(v));
'
{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","type":"array","prefixItems":[{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"}]}
[]           zod: false json-schema: true
["a"]        zod: false json-schema: true
["a",1]      zod: true  json-schema: true
["a",1,2]    zod: false json-schema: true
["a","b"]    zod: false json-schema: false
Note on other libraries
ArkType 2.2.3 emits minItems: 2 and items: false alongside prefixItems for the same shape, in the same 2020-12 dialect. TypeBox 0.34.52 emits additionalItems: false, minItems: 2 and maxItems: 2 in draft-07. Both agree with their own validator on all five probes above, so the constraint is expressible in both dialects.

A related case, in the same conversion: z.tuple([z.string()], z.number()) — a tuple with a rest element — emits {"prefixItems":[{"type":"string"}],"items":{"type":"number"}}, which accepts [] while Zod rejects it. minItems: 1 would close that one.

The probe table above was produced with schema-parity, a differential harness that runs a validator and its emitted JSON Schema over the same generated values and reports where they disagree.

raw.title: zod v4 `z.iso.datetime()` emits empty alternation (`||`) that breaks strict JSON Schema compilers
Add a deterministic API for comparing schema input compatibility
raw.body:
### Use case

We use Zod schemas as runtime input contracts and need to review schema evolution automatically. Given an old schema and a new schema, we want to determine whether every input accepted by the old schema is still accepted by the new schema.

A stricter mode could also verify that inputs accepted by the old schema produce the same parsed output under the new schema.

For example:

```ts
inputCompatible(z.null(), z.number().nullish()); // compatible

inputCompatible(z.string(), z.string().min(5)); // incompatible

inputCompatible(
  z.strictObject({ a: z.string() }),
  z.strictObject({
    a: z.string(),
    b: z.number().optional(),
  }),
); // compatible

inputCompatible(
  z.strictObject({ a: z.string() }),
  z.strictObject({
    a: z.string(),
    b: z.number(),
  }),
); // incompatible
```

A result such as `"compatible" | "incompatible" | "unknown"` would work well. `unknown` is expected for arbitrary refinements, transforms, custom schemas, or any construct the comparator cannot prove. The important property is that the result is deterministic and never guesses or relies on sampled inputs.

### Existing APIs

`.safeExtend()` checks assignability of the inferred TypeScript types, not runtime input compatibility. For example, replacing `z.string()` with `z.string().min(5)` passes its type check even though it narrows accepted input.

`z.toJSONSchema(schema, { io: "input" })` provides a useful representation, but it does not compare schemas and cannot represent every Zod construct without losing semantics.

`_zod.def` can be traversed, but consumers still have to implement and maintain Zod's runtime semantics themselves.

Would Zod be open to either a supported comparator for the deterministically comparable subset, or a normalized public representation and helper APIs intended for building one?

I'm not attached to this API shape. If Zod already has a canonical extension point, or if the maintainers prefer another way to check compatibility, I'm happy to use that instead.

Related: #1372

### Disclosure

This feature request was drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by me before posting.

raw.title: Support hierarchical semantic data for schema reflection
v4: locales other than `en` ignore the `exact` flag on `too_small` / `too_big`
raw.body:
#6177 fixed the English locale so `.length()` / `.size()` failures read "exactly N" instead of range wording. The other 49 locales still ignore `issue.exact`:

```ts
z.config(fr());
z.string().length(4).safeParse("abc");
// → "Trop petit : chaîne doit avoir >=4 caractères"
// want: wording that says the length must be exactly 4
```

Not wrong — `.length(4)` on a 3-character string really does violate `>=4` — but it understates the constraint, which is the whole point of #6176.

The fix is one line per locale, in the same slot `en` uses:

```ts
const adj = issue.exact ? "exactly " : issue.inclusive ? "<=" : "<";
```

Two groups, and the split matters for how much of this needs a translator:

- **44 locales render the comparator as a language-neutral operator** (`<=` / `<`; `fr-CA` uses `≤`). These are mechanical — `issue.exact ? "==" : ...` needs no translation at all.
- **5 locales translate the comparator into prose** and need a real word for "exactly": `ca` (`com a màxim`), `ja` (`以下である`), `ko` (`이하`), `lt` (`ne didesnis kaip`), `th` (`ไม่เกิน`).

`kh` and `ua` are deprecated aliases for `km` and `uk`, so they need nothing.

Worth deciding up front whether the operator locales get `==N` or a translated "exactly N" — the first is one sweep and no translators, the second reads better but needs 44 translations.

Only `$ZodCheckLengthEquals` and `$ZodCheckSizeEquals` set `exact`, so the reachable surface is `.length()` on strings and arrays and `.size()` on sets and maps. No locale test currently covers those; they all exercise `.min()` / `.max()` only.

raw.title: z.url(), z.ipv6() and z.cidrv6() accept ASCII tab/newline because the URL parser deletes them
raw.body:
`z.url()`, `z.httpUrl()`, `z.ipv6()` and `z.cidrv6()` all validate by calling `new URL()` and treating "didn't throw" as valid. Step 2 of the WHATWG basic URL parser **deletes** every ASCII tab, LF and CR from the input before parsing — it flags a validation error but recovers rather than failing — so `new URL()` succeeds on strings containing them and reports on a string that isn't the one it was given.

On 4.4.3:

```ts
z.ipv6().parse("::1\n");                    // "::1\n"     — net.isIPv6() says false
z.cidrv6().parse("::1\n/64");               // "::1\n/64"
z.url().parse("https://exa\nmple.com");     // "https://exa\nmple.com"
z.httpUrl().parse("https://exa\nmple.com"); // "https://exa\nmple.com"
```

The host case is the sharp one: `new URL("https://exa\nmple.com").host` is `example.com`, so the string Zod validated and the string Zod returned are URLs pointing at different hosts.

Tab, LF and CR are the only characters with this property. I enumerated all 32 C0 controls at host, path, query, fragment, leading and trailing positions: every other one is either percent-encoded (`https://example.com/pa%00th`) or rejected, and U+0009/U+000A/U+000D are the only three that can be injected into the **host** and still validate.

It also breaks a self-consistency invariant — `regexes.ipv6` is still emitted as the `pattern` by `toJSONSchema()`, and it rejects these:

```ts
new RegExp(z.toJSONSchema(z.ipv6()).pattern).test("::1\n"); // false
z.ipv6().safeParse("::1\n").success;                        // true
```

I scanned every code point 0x0000–0x10FFFF inserted into `::1` and `::1/64`: `z.ipv6()` disagrees with `net.isIPv6` on exactly those three characters and nothing else.

`isValidBase64` already handles the identical hazard one section down — "atob ignores whitespace, so reject it up front" — so the shape of the fix is settled by precedent: scan for `[\t\n\r]` ahead of each `new URL()` call. Happy to open a PR.

raw.title: redos.test.ts is flaky: both tests decide from wall-clock timing
raw.body:
`redos.test.ts` (added in #6347) fails intermittently on a clean `main`. Both of its tests decide pass/fail from wall-clock timing, so CPU contention from parallel test files flips them. It reproduced for me on `ead9fcb3` in 2 of 6 full-suite runs, and passes every time the file is run on its own — which also means `pnpm test` in the pre-push hook rejects unrelated pushes.

The two failures look different but share a cause.

**1. `no built-in pattern is ReDoS-vulnerable`**

```
AssertionError: expected [ …(3) ] to deeply equal []
+   "extendedDuration (vulnerable): ^[-+]?P(?!$)..."
+   "browserEmail (vulnerable): ^[a-zA-Z0-9.!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+@..."
+   "datetime(null,false,false) (unknown): ^(?:(?:\d\d[2468][048]..."
```

Two problems on this line:

```ts
if (result.status !== "safe") vulnerable.push(...)
```

`unknown` means the checker gave up, not that the pattern is vulnerable, so it should never fail the test. And `recheck`'s fuzz checker derives `vulnerable` from how long an attack string runs, which makes the verdict a function of available CPU. Squeezing `attackTimeout` reproduces it deterministically on an idle machine:

```
fuzz  browserEmail      10000ms=safe     1000ms=safe        100ms=safe        10ms=safe   1ms=vulnerable
fuzz  extendedDuration  10000ms=unknown  1000ms=vulnerable  100ms=vulnerable  10ms=vulnerable
auto  email             10000ms=safe     1000ms=vulnerable  100ms=vulnerable  10ms=safe   1ms=safe
```

The verdicts are not even monotonic in the budget, which is what you would expect from a timing artifact rather than a structural property.

The flagged patterns are not actually vulnerable. Matching each against adversarial input scales linearly — doubling the input roughly doubles the time, and the worst case is well under a millisecond:

```
browserEmail   len=204 0.410ms   len=804 0.010ms   len=3204 0.041ms   len=6404 0.071ms
extendedDuration  len=102 0.512ms   len=402 0.020ms   len=1602 0.069ms   len=3202 0.137ms
```

**2. `emoji rejects a backtracking payload in linear time`**

```
AssertionError: expected 111.56520799999998 to be less than 100
```

This one asserts a bare `performance.now()` budget of 100ms on a single cold call. The fixed pattern actually matches that payload in ~0.2ms, and stays flat out to 200 emoji, so the 100ms threshold sits close to JIT and scheduler noise while the real signal — the exponential version took ~1.9s — is four orders of magnitude away.

I have a fix and will open a PR: stop treating `unknown` as a failure and re-confirm any `vulnerable` verdict with a generous `attackTimeout` before failing, and warm up the emoji measurement before timing it against a threshold with real headroom. Verified that the first change still catches `^(a+)+$`, `^(a|a)*$`, `^([a-zA-Z0-9]+)*@x$` and `^(\w+\s?)*$`, so detection strength is unchanged.

fromJSONSchema: propertyNames with enum is treated as required keys
raw.body:
### Summary

`z.fromJSONSchema()` converts an object schema that constrains its keys with
`propertyNames: { enum: [...] }` into a Zod schema where each enum value becomes a
**required** property. `propertyNames` restricts which key *names are allowed*; it
does not make any key *required*. As a result, a valid object that contains only a
subset of the allowed keys is incorrectly rejected.

### Zod version

`zod@4.4.3` (Node 20)

### Reproduction

```js
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = {
  type: "object",
  propertyNames: { enum: ["a", "b"] },
  additionalProperties: { type: "string" },
};

const zodSchema = z.fromJSONSchema(schema);

// `{ a: "x" }` is valid against the JSON Schema (an allowed key, string value),
// but Zod rejects it:
zodSchema.parse({ a: "x" });
// ✖ ZodError: [{ path: ["b"], code: "invalid_type",
//     message: "Invalid input: expected string, received undefined" }]
```

### What's happening

Round-tripping the converted schema back through `z.toJSONSchema()` shows the enum
property names were turned into `required`:

```jsonc
{
  "type": "object",
  "propertyNames": { "type": "string", "enum": ["a", "b"] },
  "additionalProperties": { "type": "string" },
  "required": ["a", "b"]   // ← injected; not present in the source schema
}
```

### Expected

- `{ a: "x" }` and `{ b: "y" }` should pass (as should `{}`, unless `minProperties`
  or an explicit `required` say otherwise).
- Only keys *not* in `["a", "b"]` should fail (via `propertyNames`).
- No property should be required unless it appears in the schema's own `required`.

### Notes

This looks like the object-keyword sibling of #6200 (`fromJSONSchema` requiring
`prefixItems` tuple elements when `minItems` is omitted) — both over-require
members that the source schema leaves optional.

raw.title: `zod/mini`: `merge()` type and runtime signatures are inverted
raw.body:
`z.mini.merge()` declares a schema-to-schema signature but forwards to `util.extend()`, which requires a plain shape. The call that typechecks throws at runtime, and the call that runs is a type error. There's no way to call it that satisfies both.

```ts
import * as m from "zod/mini";

const A = m.object({ a: m.string() });
const B = m.object({ b: m.string() });

m.merge(A, B);                  // typechecks; throws at runtime
m.merge(A, { b: m.string() });  // works at runtime; type error TS2353
```

On `zod@4.4.3`:

```
merge(schema, schema) THROWS: Invalid input to extend: expected a plain object
merge(schema, shape) : [ 'a', 'b' ]
```

Under `tsc --noEmit --strict` (5.9.3 and 7.0.2 agree):

```
error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties,
  and 'b' does not exist in type 'ZodMiniObject<...>'
```

## Cause

`mini/schemas.ts:921` declares only the schema-to-schema overload, so the implementation signature isn't publicly callable:

```ts
/** @deprecated Identical to `z.extend(A, B)` */
export function merge<T extends ZodMiniObject, U extends ZodMiniObject>(
  a: T,
  b: U
): ZodMiniObject<util.Extend<T["shape"], U["shape"]>, T["_zod"]["config"]>;
export function merge(schema: ZodMiniObject, shape: any): ZodMiniObject {
  return util.extend(schema, shape);
}
```

`util.extend` guards on `isPlainObject` and throws (`core/util.ts:659`).

Mini only. Classic calls `util.merge` (`classic/schemas.ts:1555`) and `A.merge(B)` works. Present since the Zod 4 commit 85928549, unchanged in 4.4.3. `mini/tests/object.test.ts` has no `merge` case.

## Two fixes, not equivalent

Correcting the overload to `(schema, shape)` matches the `@deprecated Identical to z.extend(A, B)` note above it, with no runtime change. It breaks `merge(A, B)` at compile time, but that call already throws, so the failure just surfaces earlier.

Switching the body to `util.merge` makes the advertised signature true, matches classic and Zod 3, and picks up `b`'s `catchall`. It breaks JS callers passing a plain shape, which is the form that works today. Not silently: `checks: b._zod.def.checks ?? []` (`core/util.ts:713`) is eager, so it throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'def')` at the call. Still a runtime change to a shipped API.

`merge` is deprecated and absent from `api.mdx`, so the first is the conservative read. Which would you prefer? Happy to open a PR with a test either way.

raw.title: `encode` ignores `default`?
raw.body:
I'm not sure if it's intended or a problem, but **`encode` does not fill `default` values if not provided**:

```typescript
z.object({ optional: z.number().default(1) }).encode({}) // Invalid input: expected number, received undefined
```

IMO that's a bug because it accepts data which does not conform to the schema. In other words:
```typescript
const schema = z.object({ optional: z.number().default(1) })
schema.encode(schema.decode({})) // works
schema.decode(schema.encode({})) // doesn't
```

At the very least I think the type of `encode` should be fixed so that it won't allow wrong data, just like `decode` would do in this case.

raw.title: fromJSONSchema date-time rejects valid RFC 3339 offsets
raw.body:
`fromJSONSchema({ type: "string", format: "date-time" })` currently maps to `z.iso.datetime()` and rejects valid RFC 3339 timestamps with numeric UTC offsets.

```ts
const schema = z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "string", format: "date-time" });

schema.parse("2026-07-29T14:30:00Z"); // accepted
schema.parse("2026-07-29T16:30:00+02:00"); // rejected
```

JSON Schema defines `date-time` using RFC 3339, where both `Z` and numeric offsets are valid. A local timestamp without an offset should remain invalid.

The mapping can preserve that behavior by using `z.iso.datetime({ offset: true })`. Authored JSON Schema constraints such as `pattern` should continue to compose with the format check.

formatError and treeifyError throw TypeError when an issue path contains inherited Object.prototype names (__proto__, constructor, toString, ...)
raw.body:
### Summary

`z.formatError()` and `z.treeifyError()` both throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')` when any issue path element is a name inherited from `Object.prototype`: `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, etc.

These paths are reachable through `ctx.addIssue({ path: [...] })` in `.check()` / `.superRefine()`, and more generally whenever user-controlled keys end up in an issue path (for example record or dynamic-key validation). For an API that formats validation errors from untrusted input, this is a crash vector.

### Reproduction (zod 4.4.3, Node 22)

```ts
import * as z from "zod";

const schema = z.object({ data: z.string() }).superRefine((val, ctx) => {
  ctx.addIssue({ code: "custom", message: "invalid value", path: ["toString"] });
});

const result = schema.safeParse({ data: "hello" });

z.treeifyError(result.error); // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')
z.formatError(result.error);  // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')
```

I ran this for all five names (`__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`) against both functions on the published 4.4.3 build: all 10 combinations throw.

### Root cause

Both functions build their output trees on plain object literals and test node existence with truthy / nullish checks, which see inherited members.

`formatError` (`packages/zod/src/v4/core/errors.ts`):

```ts
curr[el] = curr[el] || { _errors: [] };
```

When `el` is `"toString"`, `curr[el]` is the inherited function, so the node is never created and `curr[el]._errors.push(...)` throws. When `el` is `"__proto__"`, plain assignment goes through the inherited setter and mutates the object's prototype instead of creating an own property.

`treeifyError` has the same class of bug:

```ts
curr.properties[el] ??= { errors: [] };
```

`properties["constructor"]` is not nullish, so `??=` never assigns and traversal walks into `Object.prototype` members.

### Fix

Guard node creation with an own-property check (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`) and create nodes with `Object.defineProperty` so that `__proto__` becomes a real own data property instead of hitting the prototype setter. This fixes the crash for all inherited names and prevents prototype mutation for `__proto__`.

I have a patch covering both `formatError` and `treeifyError` with regression tests for all five names on both functions (36 tests passing locally). Happy to open a PR.

### Related open PRs

#6083, #6139, and #6181 each address `formatError`, but as far as I can tell none of them cover `treeifyError`, which fails identically (verified on 4.4.3 as above). Filing this issue per CONTRIBUTING so there is a single reference for the full scope, with credit to those PRs for prior art on the `formatError` side.

Add support for RFC3339 full-time in z.iso.time()
raw.body:
## Problem

`z.iso.time()` validates RFC3339 `partial-time`, explicitly rejecting timezone offsets.

However, OpenAPI defines

```yaml
type: string
format: time
```

as RFC3339 `full-time`. As a result, valid OpenAPI values like

```text
10:15:30Z
10:15:30+02:00
```

cannot be validated using the built-in ISO validators.

## Use case

I'm using [Hey API](https://heyapi.dev/) to generate Zod schemas from an OpenAPI specification.

For most OpenAPI formats there is a corresponding Zod validator, but `format: time` currently has no equivalent because `z.iso.time()` implements `partial-time` instead of `full-time`.

This makes it impossible to generate a correct validator for an OpenAPI schema like:

```yaml
type: string
format: time
```

without resorting to a custom regex or `.refine()`.

## Possible solutions

Some possible APIs could be:

```ts
z.iso.time({ offset: true })
```

(similar to `z.iso.datetime({ offset: true })`)

or

```ts
z.iso.fullTime()

```

## Conclusion

Since OpenAPI and Zod are commonly used together, it would be great if OpenAPI's standard format: time could be mapped directly to a built-in Zod validator without requiring custom validation logic.

Related to #5542

raw.title: fromJSONSchema requires prefixItems tuple elements when minItems is omitted
raw.body:
## Summary

`fromJSONSchema` converts JSON Schema tuple-style array schemas into Zod required tuples. As a result, arrays shorter than the number of positional schemas are rejected even when the JSON Schema does not set `minItems`.

In JSON Schema, `prefixItems` / draft-7 array-form `items` constrain the elements that are present. They do not make every positional schema required unless `minItems` says so.

## Code path

- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: `prefixItems` is mapped to `z.tuple(...)`.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: draft-7 array-form `items` is also mapped to `z.tuple(...)`.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/tests/from-json-schema.test.ts`: the current `prefixItems` test expects a shorter array to throw, which appears stricter than JSON Schema semantics.

## Steps to reproduce

Checked against `912f0f51b0ced654d0069741e7160834dca742ee`.

### Draft 2020-12 `prefixItems`

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  $schema: "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  type: "array",
  prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }],
});

console.log(schema.safeParse([]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok"]).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
false
true
```

Expected output:

```txt
true
true
```

### Draft-7 array-form `items`

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  $schema: "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  type: "array",
  items: [{ type: "string" }],
  additionalItems: false,
});

console.log(schema.safeParse([]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok"]).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse(["ok", "extra"]).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
false
true
false
```

Expected output:

```txt
true
true
false
```

## Expected behavior

Without `minItems`, shorter arrays should be valid as long as every present positional item satisfies its schema.

For example:

- `prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }]` should accept `[]` and `["ok"]`.
- draft-7 `items: [{ type: "string" }], additionalItems: false` should accept `[]` and `["ok"]`, but reject `["ok", "extra"]`.

## Actual behavior

The generated Zod schema rejects `[]` because `z.tuple([z.string()])` requires the first tuple element to be present.

## Existing coverage

Related open PRs exist, but they appear to cover the trailing/rest side rather than the shorter-array side:

- #6020 fixes open-by-default tuple rest behavior for omitted `items` / `additionalItems`.
- #6023 fixes boolean `true` rest behavior for `items: true` / `additionalItems: true`.

Both directions are related, but adding `.rest(...)` to `z.tuple([z.string()])` still leaves the first tuple element required, so arrays shorter than the prefix length remain rejected unless the fix also changes required-prefix handling.

#6193 / #6194 are about `toJSONSchema()` emitting length constraints for closed Zod tuples, which is the opposite conversion direction.

## Suggested fix

When JSON Schema does not set `minItems` to require all positional schemas, avoid representing `prefixItems` / array-form `items` as a required-length Zod tuple directly.

The converted schema should:

- validate each present positional element against its corresponding schema;
- allow shorter arrays down to the JSON Schema `minItems` value, defaulting to `0`;
- still enforce `items:false` / `additionalItems:false` for elements beyond the positional schema list;
- preserve typed rest behavior when `items` / `additionalItems` is a schema object.

## Suggested tests

- 2020-12 `prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }]` with no `minItems` accepts `[]`.
- 2020-12 `prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }, { type: "number" }]` with no `minItems` accepts `[]` and `["ok"]`.
- A present prefix item with the wrong type still fails, e.g. `[1]` for `{ type: "string" }`.
- draft-7 `items: [{ type: "string" }], additionalItems:false` accepts `[]` and `["ok"]`, but rejects `["ok", "extra"]`.
- Adding `minItems: 1` rejects `[]`, while adding `minItems: 2` rejects arrays shorter than two items.

---
Submitted with Codex.

raw.title: fromJSONSchema ignores additionalProperties:false when patternProperties is present
raw.body:
## Summary

`fromJSONSchema` accepts object properties that match neither `properties` nor `patternProperties` when the source JSON Schema sets `additionalProperties: false`, as long as `patternProperties` is present. This makes the generated Zod schema more permissive than the source JSON Schema.

## Code path

- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: the `patternProperties` branch builds loose records and returns from that branch.
- `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/from-json-schema.ts`: the later `additionalProperties === false` handling is only reached when the earlier `patternProperties` branch is not taken.

## Steps to reproduce

Checked against `912f0f51b0ced654d0069741e7160834dca742ee`.

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  type: "object",
  patternProperties: {
    "^S_": { type: "string" },
  },
  additionalProperties: false,
});

console.log(schema.safeParse({ S_name: "ok" }).success);
console.log(schema.safeParse({ X_A: false }).success);
```

Actual output:

```txt
true
true
```

## Expected behavior

The second parse should fail. `X_A` does not match `^S_`, so it is an additional property. With `additionalProperties: false`, JSON Schema rejects properties that match neither `properties` nor `patternProperties`.

Expected output:

```txt
true
false
```

## Actual behavior

The generated Zod schema accepts `{ X_A: false }`.

## Existing coverage

I found related but not equivalent coverage:

- #5449 covered adding general `patternProperties` support.
- #5702 covers an `allOf` + `additionalProperties: false` interaction.

I did not find an issue or PR covering the `patternProperties` + `additionalProperties: false` interaction above.

## Suggested fix

Apply `additionalProperties` after accounting for keys matched by `properties` and `patternProperties`, instead of returning from the `patternProperties` branch before the `additionalProperties` logic runs.

## Suggested tests

- `fromJSONSchema({ type: "object", patternProperties: { "^S_": { type: "string" } }, additionalProperties: false })` accepts `{ S_name: "ok" }`.
- The same schema rejects `{ X_A: false }`.
- A matching pattern key with the wrong value type, such as `{ S_name: 1 }`, still fails.

---

CI: `pnpm build` fails on every PR since TypeScript 7.0.2 became `latest` (zshy crash)
raw.body:
### Summary

Every CI run of `test.yml` fails at `pnpm build` since 2026-07-08, on all PRs — including docs-only changes. The cause is external: TypeScript 7.0.2 was published to npm's `latest` tag on 2026-07-08 15:55 UTC, a few hours after the last green run on `main` (06:32 UTC that day).

### Mechanism

The test job installs the matrix TypeScript before building:

```yaml
- run: pnpm add typescript@${{ matrix.typescript }} -w
- run: pnpm build
```

`zshy@0.7.2` declares `peerDependencies: { typescript: ">5.5.0" }` and resolves the workspace TypeScript. With `typescript@latest` now resolving to 7.0.2 (the Go-native compiler, which no longer ships the TS 5.x JS compiler API), zshy crashes:

```
»  Build failed: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'readFile')
ERR_PNPM_RECURSIVE_RUN_FIRST_FAIL  zod@4.4.3 build: `zshy --project tsconfig.build.json`
```

Reproduces locally on `main` (912f0f51):

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm add typescript@latest -w   # installs 7.0.2
pnpm build                      # zshy: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'readFile')
```

Reverting to the lockfile's pinned TypeScript makes the build pass again.

Note the "TypeScript 5.5" matrix job is not independently broken — its `pnpm build` step is `cancelled` by matrix fail-fast when the `latest` job dies, so both jobs show red for one root cause.

### Possible directions

- Build with the repo's pinned TypeScript by moving `pnpm build` above the `pnpm add typescript@…` step, so the matrix TS only applies to the test/typecheck phase (which is the matrix's purpose). `pnpm test` under TS 7 may surface further issues, but they'd be the real signal rather than a toolchain crash.
- Cap the matrix at `typescript@5` until zshy supports TS 7.
- TS 7 support in zshy itself.

Happy to send a PR for the workflow reorder if that's the preferred route.

raw.title: v4: `.length()` / `.size()` error messages ignore the `exact` flag
raw.body:
## Zod version

v4.4.3

## Minimal reproduction

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

z.string().length(4).parse("abc");
```

## Expected

Since `.length(4)` represents an exact constraint, the error message should indicate that the expected length is **exactly 4**, as it did in Zod v3.

## Actual

The error message uses range wording (e.g. `>=4` / `<=4`), even though the generated issue already contains `exact: true`.

## Additional context

While investigating this, I found that:

* `exact: true` is assigned for fixed-length validations in `core/checks.ts`.
* `exact` is part of the `too_small` / `too_big` issue types.
* None of the v4 locale renderers currently use `issue.exact` when formatting messages.
* The v3 English locale did use `issue.exact` to produce messages such as "exactly 4".
* I couldn't find an existing issue or PR covering this behavior.

Before opening a PR, I'd like to confirm whether this is an unintended regression. If so, I'd be happy to submit a focused PR updating the English locale together with the relevant tests.

Take the built in example https://zod.dev/codecs?id=jsonschema#jsonschema. The only reason this type checks is because `JSON.parse`'s return type is an implicit-any. The refinement is then done by the provided schema. I posit therefore, that `decode` really should return `unknown` since it is up to the next schema in the codec chain to verify the type, not the decode step.

toJSONSchema(schemaRegistry, opts) is very slow with a large registry
raw.body:
As I add more types to a schema registry, calling `toJSONSchema` on that registry gets very slow, growing much faster than the growth in the size of the registry.

In a private repo I have, a registry with only about 3000 types in it takes 30 seconds to process on a MacBook M3.

I've collected some perf dumps, and the problem might be coming from one or both of these places:

### Finalize iteration

`finalize` is called on every schema, but for each schema it goes through all of the refs and checks each one:

https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/core/to-json-schema.ts#L449

A lot of that ends up being noop, as everything only needs to be procesesd once.  But it's still building all of those new arrays for iteration and revisiting every member of `ctx.seen` many times over.

When I hack my copy of zod to only run this loop once per context, the schema generation time for my example goes down from about 30s to about 18s.

### Nested parent computation

When a schema has a parent, registry get walks the chain recursively to get ancestor data:

https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/zod/src/v4/core/registries.ts#L65

This data can be recomputed many times as registry get is called many times, even though no registry data is written during the process.

When I add a subclass of $ZodRegistry that can cache the results of these get calls, the schema generation time for my example goes down from about 30s to about 20s.

raw.title: ability to define inline non-empty array which is expressed in its inferred type (in v4)
raw.body:
## Feature request
The change in `z.array()`'s `.nonempty()` between zod v3 and v4 (see [migration guide](https://zod.dev/v4/changelog?id=changes-nonempty-type#changes-nonempty-type)) causes the inferred type to no longer express that the array contains at least one element `T[]` vs. `[T, ...T[]]`.

The proposed solution in the migration guide is to use `z.tuple([elementSchema], elementSchema)`. Please note that this requires to repeat the element schema. In case it's a non-trivial element schema, it's hard to read and maintain in case it is defined inline. Essentially, this forces the element schema to be stored non-inline, in a variable, which also impacts readability.

I'd like to request the feature to be able to define a schema for a non-empty array inline, without repeating the element schema.

## Related tickets
There are already 2 issues about this change in inferred type:
* https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/5253
* https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/4888

Please note that the feature request in my issue is not necessarily about the change in inferred type, but about the ability to define an (inline) schema for non-empty arrays without repeating the element's sub-schema.

## Proposed solution options
* Change the inferred type of `z.array()`'s `.nonempty()` from `T[]` to `T[] & [T, ...T[]]`.
* Add a new function to `z.array()`, e.g. `.withAtLeastOneElement()` which behaves like `.nonempty()`, but having inferred type   `T[] & [T, ...T[]]`.
* Introduce a helper, e.g. `z.nonEmptyArray(elementSchema)`, which will behave the same as
  * either: `z.array(elementSchema).nonempty()`, but then with the inferred type of `T[] & [T, ...T[]]` or just `[T, ...T[]]`
  * or: `z.tuple([elementSchema], elementSchema)`

raw.title: treeifyError throws TypeError when an issue path contains a key inherited from Object.prototype (e.g. toString)
raw.body:
`treeifyError` throws a `TypeError` whenever a validation issue's `path` contains a segment whose name matches a property inherited from `Object.prototype` (for example `toString`, `valueOf`, `constructor`, or `hasOwnProperty`).

Minimal reproduction:

```
import zod, { treeifyError } from 'zod';

const schema = zod.object({ toString: zod.string() });
const result = schema.safeParse({}); // success: false

if (!result.success) {
    treeifyError(result.error); // throws TypeError
}
```

The parse correctly fails: `{}.toString` resolves to the inherited `Object.prototype.toString` function, so the `toString` field is reported as `invalid_type (expected string, received function)` with `path: ["toString"]`. That part is expected. The bug is that `treeifyError` then throws while building the tree:

```
node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:113
                        curr.errors.push(mapper(issue));
                                    ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'push')
    at processError (node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:113:37)
    at treeifyError (node_modules/zod/v4/core/errors.js:120:5)
```

Root cause:

`treeifyError` builds the tree using a plain object as a dictionary:

```
curr.properties ?? (curr.properties = {});
(_a = curr.properties)[el] ?? (_a[el] = { errors: [] });
curr = curr.properties[el];
```

When the path segment `el` is an `Object.prototype` key, `curr.properties[el]` returns the inherited member (e.g. the `toString` function) instead of `undefined`. The `??` short-circuits, so the node is never created, and `curr` is assigned the inherited function which has no `errors` array. The following `curr.errors.push(...)` then throws.
A null-prototype object (`Object.create(null)`) or a `Map` for `properties`, or an `Object.hasOwn` guard, would fix it.

Environment:
zod: 4.4.3
Node.js: v24.15.0

regexes.domain is missing RFC 1035 length limits
raw.body:
## Context

`regexes.domain` (used by `z.httpUrl()` for the URL host check) currently has no length anchors:

```ts
export const domain: RegExp = /^([a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}$/;
```

vs. `regexes.hostname` (used by `z.hostname()`), which does enforce the RFC 1035 limits:

```ts
export const hostname: RegExp =
  /^(?=.{1,253}\.?$)[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?(?:\.[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[-0-9a-zA-Z]{0,61}[0-9a-zA-Z])?)*\.?$/;
```

So `z.httpUrl()` accepts hosts that exceed the 253-character total or have non-TLD labels longer than 63 characters, while `z.hostname()` rejects them.

## Question

Is this an intentional looseness for `z.httpUrl()` (since RFC 3986 / WHATWG URL doesn't itself impose DNS length limits, even though the underlying DNS does), or a gap worth closing?

If the latter, the fix is small — adding a `(?=.{1,253}\.?$)` lookahead and capping the TLD with a `{2,63}` quantifier. Happy to follow up with a PR if there's interest.

## Note

This is independent from #5963 (underscore support, currently open), but it'd be cleaner to land that first to avoid noisy rebases.

raw.title: redos checker test fails on Windows: recheck-jar path uses forward-slash regex on backslash paths
raw.body:
## Summary

`src/v4/classic/tests/datetime.test.ts > redos checker` fails on every Windows contributor's machine with:

```
Error: Invalid or corrupt jarfile C:\Users\<…>\node_modules\recheck-jar\package.json
```

Linux CI is green; the bug is purely platform-specific path handling in `recheck`'s self-resolution logic.

## Reproduction

- Windows 10 / 11
- Any Node version
- Clean clone of zod, `pnpm install`, then:

```sh
pnpm vitest run src/v4/classic/tests/datetime.test.ts -t "redos checker"
```

Result: test fails (or times out) with the "Invalid or corrupt jarfile" error above.

## Root cause

`recheck` (the library used to assert no ReDoS-vulnerable patterns) resolves both its native binary and its bundled jar using:

```ts
require.resolve(pkg).replace(/\/package\.json$/, "/<bin>")
```

The forward-slash regex silently no-ops on Windows, where `require.resolve` returns a backslash path. `recheck` then spawns Java/exe with `package.json` itself as the executable argument — hence the corrupt-jar error.

The test itself is correct; the failure is in the optional-dependency resolution shape inside `recheck`.

## Proposed fix

[#5919](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/pull/5919) registers a small `scripts/recheck-resolve.ts` ahead of `fail-on-console` in the vitest configs. It uses `path.join` (separator-correct on every platform) to resolve:

- `recheck-{platform}-{arch}/recheck[.exe]` → exported as `RECHECK_BIN` (the native-backend override)
- `recheck-jar/recheck.jar` → exported as `RECHECK_JAR` (JVM fallback)

`recheck` short-circuits its own (buggy) resolution when either env var is set, so this is a transparent override. Pure test-infra change — no production code touched. Skips on platforms without an installed `recheck-{platform}-{arch}` or `recheck-jar` package (e.g. s390x, riscv64, FreeBSD).

## Related (different cause, same test)

These touch the same `redos checker` test but at different layers, so this issue is not a duplicate:

- #5365 — Node 22 regex engine throws a ReDoS issue inside `recheck` (closed not-planned).
- #5743 — Node 24 V8 regex perf makes the test exceed 5s timeout (closed via timeout bump).

This issue is the third axis: Windows-specific path resolution inside `recheck`'s optional-dep loader.

raw.title: z.email() should restrict length to 254 characters
raw.body:
Admittedly this is in the dark recesses of IETF errata but, in accepted errata for RFC 3696, emails should not exceed 254 characters: https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=3696

> In addition to restrictions on syntax, there is a length limit on
   email addresses.  That limit is a maximum of 64 characters (octets)
   in the "local part" (before the "@") and a maximum of 255 characters
   (octets) in the domain part (after the "@") for a total length of 320
   characters. However, there is a restriction in RFC 2821 on the length of an
   address in MAIL and RCPT commands of 254 characters.  Since addresses
   that do not fit in those fields are not normally useful, the upper
   limit on address lengths should normally be considered to be 254.


RFC 3696 is for the [checking and transformation of names](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3696) and includes a section on [email validation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3696#section-3) which in the non-corrected version says:

>   In addition to restrictions on syntax, there is a length limit on
   email addresses.  That limit is a maximum of 64 characters (octets)
   in the "local part" (before the "@") and a maximum of 255 characters
   (octets) in the domain part (after the "@") for a total length of 320
   characters.  Systems that handle email should be prepared to process
   addresses which are that long, even though they are rarely
   encountered.

So: the original limit was 320, the corrected limit is 254. Right now ZodEmail is defined as a [regex](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/c7805073fef5b6b8857307c3d4b3597a70613bc2/packages/zod/src/v4/core/schemas.ts#L452-L458) so (afaict) we'd want a fast length check before running that regex.

raw.title: Allow custom coercion logic
raw.body:
Good day!

I'm having the usecase where I want to define a JSONSchema with coercion types.
The problem is that currently there are only a few coercion types and no possibility to extend those. I want to create a validation schema for my OpenAPI Spec, where the path / query params should be validated.

The API endpoints URL looks something like this `/pathname?field=<boolean>`. So the query param `field` should represent a boolean string. The problem here is that I can't use `z.coerce.boolean()` for this, because it works with "falsy" and "truthy" values, which is a problem, because any non-empty string is truthy. So the only possible case where there schema would be a valid `false` value is the URL: `/pathname?field=` which is clearly not what I want since `/pathname?field=false` should also work. 

I'm also not able to use `z.stringbool()` as a workaround, because its internal type is `string` which is then used in the JSONSchema, but it should be a `boolean`.

So the idea is to allow a coercion customization, the API for this could look like:

```ts
z.coerce.type(z.boolean(), (v) => { /* coercion logic here */ })
z.coerce.type(z.boolean(), z.stringbool())
```

Where the first argument is the base type and the second argument is an optional coercion function or a zod type where the output is the base type. If the coercion function is not specified the default coercion takes place, so those are equivalent:
```ts
z.coerce.type(z.boolean())
z.coerce.boolean()
```

I would be ready to help / implement the feature if this is something `zod` wants to support.

raw.title: Falsy prefault() values are not emitted by toJsonSchema()
[Bug] toJSONSchema crashes on undefined schema inputs in process() and isTransforming()
raw.body:
**Zod version**: 4.3.6 (also reproduced on 4.3.5)
**Related**: #5129 (closed, but bug still present in 4.3.6)

## Description

`process()` and `isTransforming()` in `v4/core/to-json-schema.js` access `schema._zod.def` without null-checking the input. When a record schema has an undefined `valueType` (e.g., from JSON Schema → Zod conversion generating schemas with optional record types), the `recordProcessor` passes `undefined` to these functions, causing a crash.

## Error

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '_zod')
    at process (zod/v4/core/to-json-schema.js:33)
```

And after patching `process()`:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading '_zod')
    at isTransforming (zod/v4/core/to-json-schema.js:365)
```

## Crash Sites

**`process()` — line 33:**
```js
export function process(schema, ctx, _params = { path: [], schemaPath: [] }) {
    var _a;
    // ❌ No null-check — crashes if schema is undefined
    const def = schema._zod.def;
```

**`isTransforming()` — line 365:**
```js
function isTransforming(_schema, _ctx) {
    // ❌ No null-check — crashes if _schema is undefined
    const ctx = _ctx ?? { seen: new Set() };
    // ...
    const def = _schema._zod.def;
```

## Root Cause

The `recordProcessor` in `json-schema-processors.js` calls `process(def.valueType, ...)`. For some record schemas (particularly those generated from JSON Schema → Zod conversion via `json-schema-to-zod`), `def.valueType` can be `undefined`. Similarly, `isTransforming()` recursively processes `def.valueType` for record/map types without checking if it's defined first.

## Reproduction Context

This affects anyone using the MCP (Model Context Protocol) ecosystem with Zod v4:

1. `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` calls `toJSONSchema` internally to serialize tool parameter schemas for `tools/list`
2. `@payloadcms/plugin-mcp` uses `json-schema-to-zod` to convert collection JSON Schemas → Zod schemas
3. Some generated Zod record schemas have `undefined` `valueType` in their `_zod.def`
4. `tools/list` → `toJsonSchemaCompat()` → `toJSONSchema()` → `process(undefined)` → crash

## Proposed Fix

Simple null guards at the entry of both functions:

```diff
 export function process(schema, ctx, _params = { path: [], schemaPath: [] }) {
     var _a;
+    if (!schema || !schema._zod) return {};
     const def = schema._zod.def;
```

```diff
 function isTransforming(_schema, _ctx) {
+    if (!_schema || !_schema._zod) return false;
     const ctx = _ctx ?? { seen: new Set() };
```

These are safe defaults — an undefined schema has no JSON Schema representation (empty object) and is not transforming (false).

## Relationship to #5129

Issue #5129 reported the identical crash on v4.0.17 and was closed. However, we've verified the bug still exists in **v4.3.6** — the `to-json-schema.js` source has no null-checks in either function. The only change between 4.3.5 and 4.3.6 in this file is an unrelated `refSeen.def` guard at line 256.

## Impact

This blocks the entire MCP tool listing for any project using `@payloadcms/plugin-mcp` (or any MCP server that generates Zod schemas from JSON Schema) with Zod v4. The `tools/list` response fails completely, making all MCP tools inaccessible. We're currently working around this with `pnpm patch`.

raw.title: z.infer vs z.input and z.output
raw.body:
Thanks for the library and all the great work put into it! I get that naming things and keeping things consistent can be daunting, and that's also the origin of my question in this regard:

Currently in our codebase, we're using both `z.infer` and `z.output` and `z.input`. Sometimes, we're changing types, so a type might have the same input and output type and over time will receive a difference on those.

Since `z.infer` is tied to the output-type, it is possible to wrap a type in `z.infer` and later on be surprised that it doesn't match the input. The documentation just claims that you can use `z.infer` and if you need the difference, use the specific types. I would like to have a way of telling the user that he has to be explicit in what he wants.

Instead of directly linking it to `output`, it could fall to `never` if the input and output types do differ. This would make the user aware of that he needs to be explicit in what he wants, but it would still allow for those cases where it doesn't differ, to take the shared type.
```ts
type Equal<A, B> =
  [A] extends [B] ? ([B] extends [A] ? true : false) : false;

type Infer<S extends z.ZodTypeAny> =
  Equal<z.input<S>, z.output<S>> extends true ? z.output<S> : never;
```

`multipleOf` silently accepts non-multiples for small numbers (scientific notation bug in `floatSafeRemainder`)
raw.body:
`z.number().multipleOf(1e-7).safeParse(2.5e-7)` returns `{ success: true }`,  but `2.5e-7 / 1e-7 = 2.5`  (not a whole number).

Repro:
```
z.number().multipleOf(1e-7).safeParse(2.5e-7)  //  { success: true } — should be false
z.number().multipleOf(1e-7).safeParse(3.3e-7)  // { success: true } — should be false
z.number().multipleOf(1e-7).safeParse(3e-7)    // { success: true } — correct
```

Root cause: `floatSafeRemainder` in util.ts counts decimal places by splitting `val.toString()` on ".". For small numbers, JS uses scientific notation: (2.5e-7).toString() gives "2.5e-7", so the fractional part is "5e-7" (length 4) instead of the actual 8 decimal places. 

The function already handles this for the step parameter (lines 251-255) but not for val.

Suggested fix: Apply the same scientific notation regex to val.toString().

Zod version: 4.3.6

raw.title: Schemas infered to `any` type when built to `.d.ts` files.
CSP error triggered in production - `z.config({ jitless: true })` is not a great workaround
raw.body:
We see CSP errors in production builds because Zod checks `new Function("")` to determine whether unsafe-eval is possible. I don't really care that Zod _tries_ to use unsafe-eval, because our policy will disallow it. It being logged is the annoying part. Since these are reported to our violation report endpoint and clutter up (very important) security logs, we consider it a security regression.

In several issues, among which:
- https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/4461
- https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/issues/5414

the recommended solution is to set `z.config({ jitless: true })`. This needs to happen _before_ any other imports occur that use Zod, which is problematic in our SPA-case, because this forces me to load and configure Zod before anything else can happen, leading to unnecessary slowdown in startup.

Other solutions, such as re-exporting Zod, are unstable, when considering third party libraries or generated code using regular Zod imports.

The above workaround is also undesirable, because it creates a forced bootstrap/import-order workaround, it introduces an extra loading step / waterfall in app startup, which make it not feel like a long-term solution to this problem.

Instead we would like a way to disable unsafe-eval behavior without relying on import order. Ideally this is build-time or package-level flag to disable JIT outright. Alternatively, this behavior should be opt-in. I don't think anyone is in good conscience enabling unsafe-eval on production environments. There have been similar proposals in earlier issues, but those were closed without a clear path forward. Could this be reconsidered?

Schema instances have ~91 own properties → dictionary mode → ~24x slower property access vs Zod 3
raw.body:
I'm building a form library that introspects Zod schemas to auto-generate form fields, constraints, and validation. After migrating to Zod 4, I hit a significant introspection performance regression. After a lot of profiling, I tracked the root cause down to schema instance property count.

## The problem

Zod 4 schema instances end up with **~91 own properties**. This pushes them past JS engine fast-property thresholds (V8's is ~27), forcing dictionary mode for all property access — including `_def` and `_zod`.

```javascript
const schema = z.string().min(1).max(10).email();
console.log(Object.getOwnPropertyNames(schema).length); // ~91
```

The 91 properties come from:
- **~60** from the core "support prototype modifications" loop that copies prototype methods onto each instance
- **~30** from classic `ZodType` init assigning methods as own properties

Validation perf on valid data is great — this only affects introspection and construction.

## Benchmarks

Property access (same machine, Bun):

| Benchmark | Zod 3 | Zod 4 | Ratio |
|-----------|-------|-------|-------|
| `schema._def` | 298 ps | 7.23 ns | **24x** |
| `schema._zod` | — | 7.2 ns | — |
| Inline extraction | 9.52 ns | 13.08 ns | 1.4x |
| Inline extraction, cached `_zod` | — | 9.2 ns | **parity** |
| `z.string().min(1).max(10).email()` | 2.2 µs | 72.6 µs | **32x** |

Key finding: caching `schema._zod` in a local variable brings per-read performance to Zod 3 parity. The cost is in the initial property lookup on the bloated instance, not in the `_zod` object itself.

<details>
<summary>Real-world impact (form library)</summary>

Cold path (no caching):

| Operation | Zod 3 | Zod 4 | Ratio |
|-----------|-------|-------|-------|
| Field metadata extraction (string+checks) | 7.69M ops/sec | 662K ops/sec | 11.6x |
| Field metadata extraction (number+checks) | 7.26M ops/sec | 961K ops/sec | 7.5x |
| Form mount — simple (5 fields) | 53K ops/sec | 5.8K ops/sec | 9.2x |
| Form mount — complex | 13.1K ops/sec | 1.7K ops/sec | 7.7x |

With WeakMap caching on the warm path, Zod 4 reaches 10.5M ops/sec — actually faster than Zod 3. So it's cacheable, but the cold path and construction cost remain.

</details>

## Reproduction

```javascript
import * as z3 from "zod3"; // zod@3.24.4
import * as z4 from "zod";  // zod@4.x

const v3Schema = z3.string().min(1).max(10).email();
const v4Schema = z4.string().min(1).max(10).email();

// Property count
console.log("Zod 3 own props:", Object.getOwnPropertyNames(v3Schema).length);
console.log("Zod 4 own props:", Object.getOwnPropertyNames(v4Schema).length);

// Property access benchmark
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) v3Schema._def; // warmup
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) v4Schema._def;

console.time("Zod 3 _def × 10M");
for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++) v3Schema._def;
console.timeEnd("Zod 3 _def × 10M");

console.time("Zod 4 _def × 10M");
for (let i = 0; i < 1e7; i++) v4Schema._def;
console.timeEnd("Zod 4 _def × 10M");

// Construction benchmark
console.time("Zod 3 construction × 10K");
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) z3.string().min(1).max(10).email();
console.timeEnd("Zod 3 construction × 10K");

console.time("Zod 4 construction × 10K");
for (let i = 0; i < 10000; i++) z4.string().min(1).max(10).email();
console.timeEnd("Zod 4 construction × 10K");
```

## What I've already tried on my side

- `_def.type` string comparison instead of `instanceof` (instanceof is ~36x slower due to the dual-class chain)
- `_zod.bag` reads instead of iterating `_zod.def.checks` (same path `toJSONSchema` uses)
- `_zod.propValues` for discriminated unions, `_zod.values` for enums
- WeakMap caching of extraction results
- Local `_zod` caching within functions

After all that, the remaining gap is the instance property count — that's the one thing consumers can't fix.

## Workarounds for other library authors hitting this

1. Cache `schema._zod` locally: `const zod = schema._zod` then read `zod.def`, `zod.bag`
2. Use `_zod.bag` for constraints instead of iterating checks
3. Use `_def.type` instead of `instanceof`
4. WeakMap cache extraction results — schemas are immutable so this is safe

## Ideas (not sure what's feasible)

The prototype copy loop is the main contributor (~60 of the 91 properties). I tried removing it but it breaks prototype extension (`prototypes.test.ts`, `apply.test.ts`). Some thoughts:

- Could prototype extension work through a different mechanism (Proxy, `_extensions` map, etc.) that doesn't copy methods to instances?
- Could checks be plain objects instead of `$ZodCheck` class instances? Would reduce construction cost.
- Lazy bag population — only compute on first `_zod.bag` access instead of at construction.

Totally understand if the prototype extension design is intentional and this is a known tradeoff. Just wanted to surface the data in case it's useful.

## Environment

- Zod 4.x, compared against 3.24.4
- Bun (JSC) for benchmarks, also reproduced in Node 22 (V8)

raw.title: Perf: inline field-level validation in generateFastpass (JIT) for further speedups
raw.body:
## Background

While exploring Zod's performance characteristics, I built [zod-aot](https://github.com/wakita181009/zod-aot) — a compiler that inlines runtime validation logic directly into generated code. In benchmarks it shows up to **64x faster** validation compared to Zod v4's JIT.

## Why the gap exists

Zod v4's JIT (`generateFastpass`) is a great improvement — it eliminates the loop over object keys by generating a flat `new Function()`. However, each field's validation still goes through a runtime function call:

```typescript
// Zod v4 JIT — per field
shape["age"]._zod.run({ value: input["age"], issues: [] }, ctx)
```

zod-aot instead inlines the validation logic directly into the generated function body:

```typescript
// zod-aot — per field
if (typeof input["age"] !== "number") { ... }
if (!Number.isSafeInteger(input["age"])) { ... }
```

This eliminates the per-field function call overhead entirely, which is where most of the remaining perf gap comes from.

## Benchmark (Zod v4 JIT-warmed, vitest bench, 500ms warmup + 100 warmup iterations)

| Approach | 7-field object (UserSchema) | Nested object (ApiResponse, 10 items) |
|---|---|---|
| Zod v4 (JIT) | 909,000 ops/sec | 63,000 ops/sec |
| zod-aot | 4,354,000 ops/sec | 2,790,000 ops/sec |
| **Speedup** | **~4.8x** | **~44x** |

## Proposal

Extending `generateFastpass` to emit inlined `typeof` checks for primitive types (`string`, `number`, `boolean`, etc.) — falling back to `_zod.run()` for schemas that can't be statically inlined (e.g. those with custom refinements or transforms) — could bring meaningful performance gains to Zod v4 with no API changes.

This would be a **gold standard** solution: the same speedup zod-aot provides, but built directly into Zod's JIT without requiring any external tooling.

## Role of zod-aot going forward

Even if this is incorporated into Zod's JIT, zod-aot remains useful as a true **AOT (ahead-of-time) compiler** for environments where cold-start cost is unacceptable (e.g. edge functions, Cloudflare Workers) — since it requires no `new Function()` at runtime and is therefore also CSP-safe.

raw.title: perf: avoid `delete` in `finalizeIssue` to keep issue objects in V8 fast mode
raw.body:
`finalizeIssue()` uses `delete` to strip internal properties (`inst`, `continue`, `input`) from issue objects before returning them. This causes V8 to transition the objects from hidden class mode to [dictionary mode](https://v8.dev/blog/fast-properties), which makes all subsequent property access on those objects slower.

Since every finalized issue goes through this path, it affects `flattenError`, `formatError`, `treeifyError`, etc.

The fix is straightforward — destructure out the internal properties instead of deleting them, so the returned object is clean from the start. 1 function, net -1 line, all 3574 tests pass unchanged.

I benchmarked three realistic scenarios (form validation + flatten, API response + format, config + treeify) with static fixture data and saw **6-8% improvement** on the error consumption path.

We know this is small stuff, but given how widely Zod is used and that this is the hot path for error handling, these minor improvements add up.

Happy to submit a PR with the fix and benchmark if this sounds reasonable.

raw.title: Regression: Confirm field cross-validation (password match) no longer reactive in Zod 4 + RHF
raw.body:
In **Zod 3**, it was possible to implement reactive cross-field validation for password confirmation using `field.superRefine`. 

Example (Zod 3):

  .superRefine((data, ctx) => {
            if (data.confirm !== data.password) {
              ctx.addIssue({
                code: z.ZodIssueCode.custom,
                message: t('validation.passwordsMatch'),
                path: ['confirm'],
              });
            }


This worked as expected with React Hook Form and mode: "onChange":

The confirm field would show a password mismatch error reactively as the user typed

No submission was required to trigger the error

Note: This reactive feedback occurred only on the confirm field, which is the expected and natural behavior.

Problem in Zod 4

In Zod 4, ctx.parent was removed. The recommended approach is now to use object.refine() with a path to target the error:

const schema = z
  .object({
    password: z.string().min(8),
    confirmPassword: z.string(),
  })
  .refine((data) => data.password === data.confirmPassword, {
    message: "Passwords must match",
    path: ["confirmPassword"],
  });

However, when using React Hook Form with mode: "onChange":

The confirm error does not appear while typing

No mismatch feedback is shown until the form is submitted

After submit, reactive updates work, but the initial typing gives no error

This is a regression compared to Zod 3.

Expected Behavior

Cross-field validation for confirm should trigger reactively as the user types

Password mismatch errors should appear without submitting the form

Behavior should match Zod 3 superRefine experience

Environment

Zod 4.x

React Hook Form 7.x

React 19.x

Notes / Reproduction

This issue occurs even when using:

useForm({
  resolver: zodResolver(schema),
  mode: "onChange",
})

It seems to be a limitation in the interaction between Zod 4's object-level .refine() and React Hook Form's partial validation strategy.

A minimal reproduction in CodeSandbox would make this behavior easy to verify.

raw.body:
Consider the following example:

```ts
import { z } from "zod";

function sample(schema: z.ZodCoercedNumber){
    return schema.parse("123")
}

sample(z.number())
```

No type error is emitted, even though `z.number()` does not coerce strings into numbers (unlike `z.coerce.number()`). As a result, this code compiles successfully but fails at runtime, causing a silent and potentially confusing bug.

Expected behavior

Passing a `ZodNumber` where a `ZodCoercedNumber` is expected should result in a type error, since their runtime behaviors are different.

Suggestion

Introduce a stricter type distinction so that:

- `ZodCoercedNumber` is assignable to `ZodNumber` (since it is effectively a specialized version of it), but

- `ZodNumber` is not assignable to `ZodCoercedNumber`.

This would help TypeScript catch cases where coercion is required but not actually provided, preventing subtle runtime errors.

raw.body:
We already have `z.union`, `z.intersection`, and symmetric difference (via `z.xor`), why not other Set operations like:
* `.inverse` - shorter/more performant form of `z.xor([schema, z.any()])`
* `.difference` - shorter/more performant form of `z.intersection([schemaA, z.xor([schemaB, z.any()])])`
* `.isSubsetOf` - all possible values of schema A contained within those of B
* `.isSupersetOf` - all possible values of schema B contained within those of A
* `.isDisjointFrom` - possible values of each schema have no overlap

*I give no guarantee that the listed alternatives are accurate or performant*

It would also be nice to have a method that asks, "can I give any possible output of this schema as input to this other schema?", maybe called `isAssignableTo`?

One decision that needs to be made is whether the Set methods should operate on input types or output types of schemas. I was thinking that they would generally pick one (maybe inputs), but add a method for the user to select the opposite (e.g. `.matchOutputs()`) if needed.

Since Zod is TS-first, there should also be utility types that have the same effect (e.g. `z.inverseT<schema>`, `z.isSubsetOfT<schema, ifTrue = true, ifFalse = false>`), and those would be the return type of their respective methods.

The purpose of all this would be to tell what types a given schema accepts, without knowing how it was created or peeking into Zod internals.

## Summary

Add native string transformation methods for common casing patterns:

- `.capitalize()` - capitalize first letter only (`"hello world"` → `"Hello world"`)
- `.titleCase()` - capitalize first letter of each word (`"hello world"` → `"Hello World"`)

## Motivation

Currently Zod v4 provides `.toLowerCase()`, `.toUpperCase()`, and `.trim()` as native string transforms. However, capitalize and title case are equally common patterns that require verbose `.transform()` workarounds:

```typescript
// Current workaround for title case
z.string().transform((s) => s.replace(/\b\w/g, (c) => c.toUpperCase()))

// Current workaround for capitalize
z.string().transform((s) => s.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + s.slice(1).toLowerCase())
```

## Proposed API

```typescript
// Capitalize first letter
z.string().capitalize()
// "hello world" → "Hello world"

// Title case (capitalize each word)
z.string().titleCase()
// "hello world" → "Hello World"

// Standalone for Zod Mini
z.capitalize()
z.titleCase()
```

## Use Cases

- Form inputs: names, titles, addresses
- Display formatting before storing in database
- Normalizing user input

Would fit naturally alongside existing `.toLowerCase()` and `.toUpperCase()` methods.

I am using i18next with typescript (https://www.i18next.com/overview/typescript) to get intellisense for translations and rely on type safety.

  description: z.string("field.invalid").min(1, "field.required"),
});

```tsx

  {errors.description?.message && (
    {t($ => $[errors.description.message]}
  })
)
```

This is my best option so far, to keep schemas and i18n decorrelated.

Please note I am using RHF as my form manager. The library receives those errors and seems to type them itself. It would then be also responsible for properly typing error messages.
